supported_claims.text: 生 is best analyzed as an ideographic compound: an image of a sprout above a ground mark, depicting a plant emerging from soil. The lower mark 一 represents ground; neither element is identified as phonetic. The sprout is a pictorial component, not a semantic category marker.

The graphic account describes oracle-bone forms with 屮 above 一, early bronze forms retaining that arrangement, and a dot later added beneath the sprout as a decorative stroke that became a horizontal line and made the base resemble 土. Seal forms retain the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. The selected oracle and bronze illustrations are modern vector renderings, not inspected artifact photographs.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as 進, “advance,” and describes plants emerging above soil. The paleographic interpretation treats “advance” as an extended sense, rather than the graphic core.

Reported oracle-bone uses include childbirth, live or fresh birds and deer, and 生月, interpreted in one account as “following month.” These establish early uses, not an ordered development among those meanings. 生月 is disputed: “this month” and other readings have also been proposed.

Bronze and Warring States examples report 生 for giving birth, living, lifespan, and occurring or producing. Later lexicographic sources also list growth, birth or raising, life opposed to death, and production or occurrence. The evidence does not establish a secure chronological chain among these senses.

The graph 生 is reported as a phonetic loan for 姓 in an oracle-bone phrase and on a bronze inscription. This means the sign 生 was reused to write the different word 姓, not that 生’s meaning developed into “surname.” The proposed comparison has modern Mandarin shēng versus xìng and supplied Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese sraeng versus sjengH and Old Chinese *sreŋ versus *seŋ-s; these comparisons alone do not establish the historical borrowing.

The dossier supplies modern readings for 生, including Mandarin shēng, and historical pronunciation rows with distinct Middle Chinese and Old Chinese notations. It supplies no usable reading pair for 屮 and 生 as a proposed phonetic component comparison; 屮 is analyzed graphically, not phonologically.

disagreements.text: The oracle-bone phrase 生月 has competing interpretations, including “following month” and “this month” or another reading. The debate concerns the phrase’s lexical interpretation and does not prove that month terminology developed from the sprout image.
For the oracle-bone phrase 多生, one account reads 生 as 姓, while 多甥 is offered as an alternative analysis. The proposed use is a whole-graph borrowing, not a component analysis of 生.

limitations.text: The cited inscriptions support reported uses, but the dossier does not date each cited token or establish priority among the senses of birth, living, freshness, production, lifespan, and other reported uses.

The oracle-to-bronze-to-seal graphic account does not provide a dated artifact-by-artifact chain. The selected illustrations are modern digital renderings; their pixels were not visually inspected in this research.
A proposed conservative form 𤯓 and its relation to other graphs are mentioned, but the dossier’s research did not independently establish its chronology, ancestry, or a corruption history.
The supplied local readings and reconstruction rows are not independently verified against the referenced upstream character-specific pages, which were inaccessible during research.
